statutory_provisions: Penal Code s.302 (murder); a separate theft charge was also framed, section not stated in the judgment
weapon: Steel rod (blood-stained, recovered from beneath a stone slab)
evidence_type: Circumstantial: presence at house, fingerprint on plastic cover, blood-stained clothes, ornament and steel rod recoveries; identification by two witnesses; no medical or eyewitness proof of the killing
confession: Disclosure by the accused led to ornament and steel rod recoveries (page 20). The High Court treated a Section 313 answer as an admission of a fingerprint; the Supreme Court rejected that reliance as selective and unsupported.
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted; benefit of doubt given. No sentence.
high_court_outcome: Acquittal set aside on appeal; accused convicted of murder
neutral_facts: On 5 November 1990 a man unknown to the victim was looking for her house in a city and asked a passer-by for directions. The passer-by took him to a second woman, who escorted him to the victim's house. At about 1 p.m. a witness saw him at the victim's door. He said a relative was expected to come to the house; the victim replied that the relative had not arrived. That witness left before the man entered the house. That evening the victim did not come to a neighbour's house to watch television. The neighbour sent a child to call her, and the victim said relatives from her village had arrived and she had to cook for them. Another witness saw her alive at about 8.30 p.m. in the company of more than one person. The next day the victim was found dead in her house, with her belongings scattered. At the scene, an expert found chance fingerprints on a plastic cover bearing a bank's name. Later, an expert reported that the accused's fingerprint matched one of them, using a print taken from the accused on a later date. The accused's blood-stained clothes were seized when he was arrested six days after the killing. A blood sample from him could not be tested for blood group. Ornaments were recovered from several people after the accused led police to them, but none was identified as the victim's. A blood-stained steel rod, hidden under a stone slab, was recovered at the accused's instance. No identification parade was held. The relative the accused had mentioned was not questioned by investigators.
physical_harm: Death of the victim by homicide
number_of_offences: 2 charged (murder; theft of cash and ornaments); 0 finally upheld
financial_property_loss: Cash and ornaments alleged to be worth about Rs. 25,000; the ornaments were never linked to the victim
key_evidence_accepted: Accepted only in part: the accused was at best at the house around 1 p.m.; the victim was alive until about 8.30 p.m. with others present; the homicidal death. Fingerprint, blood-group, recovery and identification evidence was not accepted as proving guilt.
witness_credibility: Fingerprint expert's bona fides accepted. Identification witnesses PW-6 and PW-7 were weak (brief, fleeting sighting; identification in court about 4.5 years later). Photographer's evidence on the passbook print was inconsequential.
post_offence_conduct: High Court found absconding after the crime; the Supreme Court did not accept this as proof of guilt. Prosecution case: apprehended on 11 Nov 1990 at about 4.45 p.m.
trial_duration: offence: 5 November 1990; trial judgment: 21 January 1999; High Court: 6 July 2005; Supreme Court: 15 April 2014
legal_representation: Appellant: K. Parmeshwar, Shekhar G. Devasa, Dinesh Kumar Garg. State (Respondent): Gurudatta Ankolekar, V.N. Raghupathy
investigation_status: FIR registered; investigation completed; charge sheet filed; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: No identification parade held; accused's fingerprint taken without Magistrate's order and its source unexplained; fingerprint cover removed without panchnama; blood-stained crowbar and steel rod not sent for examination; relative not questioned; ornaments not identified; serologist report not put to accused under s.313
appeal_history: Trial court (21 Jan 1999): acquitted. High Court (6 Jul 2005): acquittal set aside, convicted. Supreme Court (15 Apr 2014): appeal allowed, accused acquitted.
defence_argument: Photographs did not show the plastic cover, so it was planted later; the fingerprint was taken on 7 November 1990 under a cover-to-hold pretext; the serologist report was not put to him; the ornament identification procedure was improper.
legal_principle_applied: Circumstantial evidence requires certainty of each circumstance; mere probabilities are insufficient. Benefit of doubt where the trial court's view is plausible and not perverse. Identification parade not mandatory. Fingerprint evidence needs a proven admitted specimen and a fair procedure.
precedent_relied_upon: Marcouix v. The Queen (1976) 1 SCR 763; Mezzo v. The Queen (1986) 1 SCR 802; Ravi Kapur v. State of Rajasthan (2012) 9 SCC 284; R. Shaji v.
